title: Financial Statement Intelligence Engine
description: Pulls 10 years of filed 10-K data for 20 US companies straight from the SEC EDGAR XBRL API, turns it into profitability, efficiency, leverage and cash-flow ratios, narrates the trends, and scores each company against published thresholds. Outputs a 23-page report.
highlights: Every figure comes from filed 10-K data via the SEC EDGAR XBRL API across 20 companies and 10 fiscal years. Nothing is hand-entered, and the spot checks tie out to the filings (NVIDIA FY2025 revenue $130.5B, Microsoft FY2025 $281.7B, Tesla 2024 $97.69B).

Most of the engineering went into making EDGAR usable. Companies migrate between GAAP tags mid-history after ASC 606, so values are merged across an ordered list of candidate tags rather than taken from the first tag that returns anything, which took NVIDIA and Tesla from 6 usable years to 10.

Oil majors and several pharma companies never tag an operating income line, so EBIT is rebuilt from pretax income plus interest expense. Without that fallback, Exxon, Chevron, J&J, Merck and Pfizer produced no usable years at all.

EPS growth is deliberately excluded from the score. A 10-K restates only the roughly three years it covers, so Apple's FY2018 EPS reads 11.91 in one filing and 2.98 in another after the 4-for-1 split. Growth is scored on revenue and net income, which splits cannot distort.

The score refuses to invent results where data is missing: unavailable metrics are dropped, the remaining weights in that pillar are renormalized, and the exclusions are disclosed on each company's page. This caught negative book equity at Home Depot and AbbVie, where a negative debt-to-equity had been clamping to a perfect leverage score and overstating AbbVie by four points.

The resulting ranking is the clearest evidence of the method's own weakness, which is the point. The top four are all asset-light software and advertising businesses while Walmart lands 18th, because absolute thresholds measure the business model more than how well the company is run. Peer-relative scoring is the next module.

Full threshold table, fiscal-year convention and six known limitations are published in the report and README, so any score can be recalculated or argued with. Backed by 13 tests covering the negative-equity, zero-interest and weight-renormalization edge cases.

title: Institutional-Style Valuation Engine
description: DCF built from a component-level WACC, cross-checked against comparable-company multiples, with bull/base/bear scenarios and Monte Carlo valuation distributions instead of a single fair-value number.
highlights: DCF forecasts revenue growth, margin, D&A, working capital and capex line by line into unlevered free cash flow, not a single-line "grow revenue X%" shortcut.
WACC is derived from its actual components (risk-free rate, beta, equity risk premium, cost of debt, effective tax rate), never hard-coded.
Comparable-company valuation cross-checks the DCF against peer P/E, EV/EBITDA, EV/Revenue and FCF yield, reporting the premium or discount to peer median.
Bull/base/bear scenarios and a WACC-vs-terminal-growth sensitivity table show how fragile the fair value actually is to each assumption.
Monte Carlo valuation treats growth, margin and WACC as distributions rather than fixed points, producing a range of intrinsic value with percentile bands instead of one number.

title: Quantitative Risk Engine
description: Market and fundamental risk quantified through VaR, Expected Shortfall, GARCH volatility forecasting and configurable stress tests, translating each shock directly into its impact on fair value and share price.
highlights: VaR computed three ways (historical, parametric, Monte Carlo) and checked against Expected Shortfall for consistency, rather than reporting one VaR number as if methodology doesn't matter.
GARCH volatility forecasts are benchmarked against realized volatility and included only where they change the risk read, not added just to look technical.
A fundamental risk score tracks margin compression, rising net debt/EBITDA and deteriorating interest coverage, kept separate from the market-risk metrics.

Stress scenarios (revenue shock, margin compression, WACC increase, rate shock, market drawdown) flow straight through into the valuation engine, so a shock shows its real effect on fair value and share price.
For multi-asset exposure, risk contribution and concentration are broken out per position rather than reported only at the portfolio level.

title: AI Financial Research Analyst (RAG)
description: A retrieval-augmented research agent that answers investment questions by calling the financial, valuation and risk engines as tools and citing the filing, page and section behind every claim.
highlights: The LLM never calculates or invents a financial figure; it calls dedicated financial-statement, valuation and risk tools and reports what they return.
RAG retrieves the actual annual-report or filing section behind an answer before the model responds, so "why did margins decline" is answered from a real disclosure, not a guess.
Every research response is labeled as source-derived fact, model-derived calculation, or AI interpretation, so a reader knows which parts to trust and which to check.
Confidence scoring and a data-freshness check let the system say "insufficient evidence" instead of producing a fluent but unsupported answer.
An audit log records what was retrieved and which tools fired for every answer, so a research conclusion can be traced back and reproduced.

title: Investment Committee Dashboard
description: A six-page decision terminal that turns financial analysis, valuation, risk and AI research into one BUY/HOLD/SELL memo, stating the explicit thresholds that would change the call.
highlights: Six pages, not one screen: overview, financial analysis, valuation, risk, AI research and an investment-committee memo, each built for a different reviewer's question.
The memo states the recommendation alongside the specific financial thresholds that would flip it, rather than a static, one-time conclusion.
Every chart on the valuation and risk pages links back to the same underlying model output the AI analyst cites, so the dashboard and the AI never disagree.
Designed to answer whether the company is healthy, what it's worth, and what could go wrong within a few minutes for someone seeing it for the first time.
